strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: unreliable minority-class pseudo-labels in semi-supervised graph learning. UNREAL combines clustering agreement, geometric ranking, and ambiguity filtering in a modular framework compatible with several GNN architectures.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering synthetic and natural imbalance, multiple backbones, large graphs, and heterophilous datasets. Several reported improvements are substantial: on Cora with GCN and imbalance ratio 10, macro-F1 increases from BIM’s 72.67 to 76.44.

The appendix provides useful pseudo-label accuracy analyses, comparisons with ordinary self-training, pseudocode, and hyperparameter ranges. Public benchmarks, a code link, and five-run reporting support reproducibility. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. A minority embedding moving from a decision boundary toward an incorrect class center can increase the defined geometric imbalance while decreasing prediction entropy. Appendix C also drops the imbalanced class priors and class-specific concentration parameters without justification. Its final bounds are internally contradictory: at D_intra = 0, the lower bound is log C while the upper bound is strictly smaller. These are substantive correctness failures in a central contribution.

Theorem 2 does not establish the claimed dependence on imbalance ratio. The experimental protocol changes labeled class counts without changing graph neighborhoods; with fixed embeddings and class centers, this need not increase minority geometric imbalance. Appendix D assumes the required relationship between imbalance and cross-class neighbors without a graph-generating model, derives proportionality to rho squared, and then concludes proportionality to rho. The claimed causal role of message passing therefore remains unsupported.

The connection between theory and algorithm is insufficiently established. DGIS uses a nearest-versus-second-nearest centroid margin, whereas Definition 1 measures distance to the true class center relative to global class separation. No approximation guarantee or direct empirical correspondence connects these quantities. Theorem 3 establishes a property of the ranking weights, not that their use reduces geometric imbalance. The transfer from the vMF analysis to the implemented MLP classifier is also unexplained.

The ablation tables contradict their interpretation. In Tables 1 and 32, every best-performing row marks both Node-Reordering and DGIS as disabled, while the text claims their combination performs best in three settings. As printed, these tables cannot substantiate the contributions of the proposed modules. Claims of uniformly superior performance also overstate the results: Table 4 reports GraphSAGE macro-F1 of 71.86 versus 73.59 for GraphENS with TAM.

Methodological originality needs clearer positioning. Appendix B acknowledges that M3S already clusters embeddings and filters pseudo-labels through agreement with classifier predictions, closely overlapping with the proposed DualPath alignment mechanism. The M3S comparison is limited to one dataset without uncertainty estimates. IceBerg, a directly relevant 2025 method discussed in the paper, is not evaluated. Stronger differentiation and controlled comparisons are needed to isolate the new contribution.

The efficiency evidence does not establish the claimed overall training cost. Appendix K permits 40–100 self-training rounds with up to 2,000 epochs per subsequent round, whereas Table 12 reports fixed-epoch training and individual selection timings rather than complete runs. End-to-end runtime and comparisons under matched training budgets are needed. Experimental reporting also inconsistently describes uncertainty as standard errors in the main text and standard deviations in the checklist.
